title: Heat: how much energy warms water?
goal: Find how the heat needed depends on the mass and on the rise in temperature.
note: The heat needed is Q = m c delta-theta. For water the specific heat capacity c is 4200 joules for each kilogram and each degree Celsius.

graphs.title: The heat needed rises in a straight line with the rise in temperature.
graphs.label: Heat needed

experiment.aim: To find how the heat needed depends on the mass and the rise in temperature of water
experiment.hypothesis: The heat needed is directly proportional to the mass and to the rise in temperature

sentences: Every substance has its own specific heat capacity. Water has a high one, so it needs a lot of heat to warm up and releases a lot as it cools.
Doubling the mass doubles the heat needed, and so does doubling the rise in temperature.
steps: Keep the mass at 2, set the rise in temperature to 20, then press Record.
Set the rise in temperature to 40, then press Record.
Set the rise in temperature to 60, then press Record.
Compare the heat needed each time the rise doubles.

predict.prompt: If the rise in temperature stays the same and the mass of water doubles, what happens to the heat needed?
predict.reveal: Set the mass to 1, then to 2, with the rise at 20, and compare the heat needed.

concept_check.question: Why does a kilogram of water need more heat than a kilogram of aluminium for the same rise in temperature?
options: Water has a higher specific heat capacity
Water has a lower specific heat capacity
concept_check.explanation: The heat needed is mass times specific heat capacity times the rise in temperature. For the same mass and rise, the larger specific heat capacity needs more heat.

hints: A bigger mass needs more heat for the same rise.
Heat equals mass times specific heat capacity times the rise.
